name_cjk: 曼陀羅華 / 朝鮮朝顔
fact: Datura contains the tropane alkaloids scopolamine, hyoscyamine and atropine; a datura-based draught (tsūsensan) was used by Hanaoka Seishū for general anaesthesia in 1804.
caution: Dilated pupils, dry mouth, racing heart and delirium; every part of the plant is toxic and the dose is unpredictable.
maomao_note: The flowers are lovely. So is the gap between 'asleep' and 'never waking up'. Measure it.

fact: Aconite root contains aconitine, which opens sodium channels and causes fatal arrhythmias; traditional medicine only uses roots processed by prolonged soaking and boiling, which hydrolyses most of the aconitine.
caution: Numb lips and tongue are the first warning; raw root is lethal in gram amounts.
maomao_note: Boil it for hours and it is a medicine. Skip the boiling and you have saved a great deal of future effort.

fact: Foxglove leaves contain cardiac glycosides (digitoxin, digoxin); William Withering published their use for dropsy in 1785, and digoxin is still prescribed for heart failure and atrial fibrillation.
caution: Very narrow margin between a dose that slows the heart and one that stops it; nausea and yellow-tinged vision are warning signs.
maomao_note: A plant that argues with the heart and sometimes wins. I would like a specimen. For study.

fact: Atropa belladonna yields atropine; its name recalls Renaissance women who used the juice to dilate their pupils for a wide-eyed look.
caution: Glossy black berries are sweet and have poisoned children; hot, dry, flushed and delirious is the classic picture.
maomao_note: Beauty by way of blindness. The court would buy it by the jar if nobody told them the second half.

fact: Ephedra stems contain ephedrine, isolated by Nagai Nagayoshi in 1885; it opens the airways and was a standard asthma drug before synthetic alternatives.
caution: Raises blood pressure and heart rate; ephedra supplements are banned in several countries after deaths.
maomao_note: Good for a tight chest. Also good for staying awake three nights grinding other things. Not recommended. Done anyway.

fact: Licorice root owes its sweetness to glycyrrhizin, roughly fifty times sweeter than sucrose, and appears in more traditional Chinese prescriptions than almost any other herb as a harmoniser.
caution: Large or long-term intake causes pseudoaldosteronism: low potassium, water retention and high blood pressure.
maomao_note: Sweet enough to hide the taste of almost anything. That is useful information in more than one direction.

fact: Panax ginseng root has been prized in East Asian medicine for over two millennia; its characteristic compounds are the ginsenosides, and wild roots once fetched more than their weight in silver.
caution: Can interact with blood thinners and diabetes medicines; not a cure-all despite the price.
maomao_note: Shaped like a little man and priced like a large house. The shape is the only part that impresses me.

fact: The dried, fluffed leaves of mugwort (Artemisia argyi) are the moxa burned on or above acupuncture points in moxibustion, a practice recorded in Chinese texts from the Han dynasty.
caution: Burning moxa causes blisters if left too long; the pollen is a common hay-fever trigger.
maomao_note: Smells like a campfire and a temple at once. Patients complain about the burn. The burn is the point.

fact: The latex of Papaver somniferum contains morphine and codeine; morphine, isolated by Friedrich Sertürner around 1804, was the first alkaloid ever purified from a plant.
caution: Strong pain relief, strong dependence; overdose stops the breathing.
maomao_note: The best painkiller in the cabinet and the hardest to put back. Lock the drawer. Then lock the key somewhere else.

fact: Lily of the valley contains the cardiac glycoside convallatoxin; all parts are toxic, including the water a cut bouquet has stood in.
caution: Looks edible to children (the red berries especially); causes vomiting and a dangerously slow heartbeat.
maomao_note: Little white bells. Ring one and the heart answers slowly. Do not drink the vase.

fact: Every part of Nerium oleander contains oleandrin and related cardiac glycosides; even smoke from burning the wood and skewers cut from its branches have caused poisoning.
caution: A single leaf can seriously poison a child; no safe culinary or household use.
maomao_note: Planted everywhere because it is pretty and nothing eats it. Nothing eats it for a reason.

fact: Cinnabar is mercury(II) sulfide, the red pigment of seals and lacquer; alchemical 'elixirs of immortality' built around it are blamed for the deaths of several Chinese emperors, including Tang rulers.
caution: Heating releases mercury vapour; chronic exposure damages nerves and kidneys.
maomao_note: The seal on an imperial order and the pill that killed an emperor are the same colour. Seals are the safer use.

fact: Basic lead carbonate was the brilliant white of cosmetics in China, Japan and Europe for centuries; lead absorbed through skin and swallowed from the lips causes anaemia, nerve damage and is especially harmful to infants.
caution: Historic 'oshiroi' poisoned courtesans and nursing babies; modern face powders use titanium or zinc oxide instead.
maomao_note: The whitest face in the pavilion and the sickest baby in it. The powder does not care about rank.

fact: Arsenic trioxide is odourless and tasteless, which made it the classic poison until the Marsh test (1836) could detect it; today the same compound is an approved treatment for acute promyelocytic leukaemia.
caution: Vomiting, rice-water diarrhoea and collapse; chronic exposure shows as skin changes and nail lines.
maomao_note: No taste, no smell, no colour. Everything a poisoner wants and everything a taster hates. I keep a list of the symptoms anyway.

fact: Honey can carry dormant Clostridium botulinum spores; adults digest them harmlessly, but in infants under one year the spores can germinate in the gut and cause infant botulism.
caution: Never feed honey to babies under twelve months; 'mad honey' from rhododendron nectar contains grayanotoxins.
maomao_note: Sweet, soothing, excellent for a cough. Also a reason a baby stops moving. Age matters. Write it on the jar.

fact: Ginger rhizome contains gingerols and shogaols; clinical trials support it for nausea, including morning sickness and motion sickness.
caution: Mild blood-thinning effect in large amounts; otherwise about as safe as a kitchen herb gets.
maomao_note: For a sick stomach, slice it thin and steep it. For a sick mood, there is nothing I can prescribe.

fact: Cassia cinnamon bark is rich in cinnamaldehyde and also contains coumarin, which is why food regulators set a tolerable daily intake for coumarin from cinnamon.
caution: A spoonful a day of cassia for months can stress the liver; Ceylon cinnamon has far less coumarin.
maomao_note: Warms the body, sweetens the medicine, and in quantity quietly annoys the liver. Most pleasant things do.

fact: Angelica sinensis root is one of the most used herbs in traditional Chinese gynaecology; it contains ligustilide and ferulic acid and is nicknamed 'female ginseng'.
caution: May increase the effect of warfarin and other blood thinners; avoid in pregnancy without advice.
maomao_note: Half the women in the rear palace could use it and the other half are already taking too much. Ask before you brew.

fact: Safflower petals give the red pigment carthamin, the source of traditional beni lip and cheek colour in Japan, and are used in Chinese medicine to 'move blood'.
caution: Traditionally avoided in pregnancy; the oil is a food, the flower is a drug.
maomao_note: Red for the lips and red for the medicine. The courtesans know the first use better than most physicians know the second.

fact: Clove buds are up to about fifteen percent eugenol, a local anaesthetic and antiseptic still used in dental cements; Han-dynasty courtiers reportedly held cloves in the mouth before addressing the emperor.
caution: Pure clove oil burns mucous membranes and is toxic to small children in teaspoon amounts.
maomao_note: Chew one before an audience and your breath is fit for an emperor. Chew ten and your tongue goes numb. Chew one.

fact: Dried chrysanthemum flowers are brewed as a cooling tea in Chinese medicine, and chrysanthemum wine is drunk at the Double Ninth festival (重陽) for long life.
caution: Allergic reactions in people sensitive to the daisy family; otherwise a gentle tea.
maomao_note: A flower for poems, festivals and tired eyes. Nothing lethal about it, which makes it restful company.

fact: Lotus seeds are eaten and prescribed as a tonic; the bitter green embryo inside (蓮子心) contains the alkaloids liensinine and neferine, and lotus seeds have germinated after more than a thousand years in dry lakebeds.
caution: Food-safe; remove the bitter heart unless you want it.
maomao_note: Pull out the green heart or the sweet soup tastes of regret. Keep the hearts. They are a medicine too.

fact: The jujube appears in the Shennong Bencao Jing and in a large share of classical formulas, where it is added to harmonise harsher herbs and protect the stomach.
caution: Food; the stone is a choking hazard and the sugar content is high.
maomao_note: The herb that makes the other herbs bearable. Every workshop needs one. Every workshop also needs someone who is not.

fact: Goji berries from Lycium barbarum are rich in zeaxanthin and have been used in Chinese medicine for the eyes and liver since antiquity.
caution: Documented interaction with warfarin; the leaves and root bark are separate drugs.
maomao_note: Red, sweet, good for the eyes. I ate a handful to confirm. Then another handful for thoroughness.

fact: Ganoderma lingzhi is listed in the Shennong Bencao Jing as a superior herb; the 'mushroom of immortality' is bitter with triterpenoids and is grown commercially on logs today.
caution: Mild blood-thinning and digestive upset in some people; immortality not among the documented effects.
maomao_note: Immortality, says the label. Bitter, says the tongue. I trust the tongue.

fact: Conium maculatum contains coniine, which causes an ascending paralysis ending in respiratory failure; Socrates was executed with a hemlock draught in 399 BC.
caution: Easily mistaken for wild carrot or parsley; the mousy smell is a clue.
maomao_note: Looks like a carrot's cousin and kills from the feet up. Philosophers are not the only ones who should check their vegetables.

fact: Castor seeds contain ricin, one of the most toxic plant proteins known, yet cold-pressed castor oil is a traditional laxative because ricin stays in the seed cake.
caution: A few chewed seeds can be fatal; the oil is safe, the seed is not.
maomao_note: The oil empties the bowels and the seed empties the house. Same plant, different drawer.

fact: The root of Rheum palmatum contains anthraquinones such as emodin and sennosides, a reliable laxative; the leaves of garden rhubarb are rich in oxalic acid and not safe to eat.
caution: Purging herb, not a food; overuse causes cramping and potassium loss.
maomao_note: Works exactly as promised, which is the problem. Prescribe with directions to the privy.

fact: Mint's menthol triggers the cold-sensing TRPM8 receptor, which is why it feels cool without lowering the temperature of anything.
caution: Concentrated menthol oil is dangerous for infants; the leaf is harmless.
maomao_note: Cools the mouth without cooling anything. A convincing lie that happens to help a headache.

fact: Chinese star anise (Illicium verum) is the industrial source of shikimic acid, the starting material for the influenza drug oseltamivir; Japanese star anise (shikimi, I. anisatum) looks alike but contains anisatin and has caused poisonings.
caution: Buy culinary star anise from a trusted source; the toxic lookalike causes seizures.
maomao_note: Two stars, one for soup and one for seizures. Count the points, smell the fruit, and still do not trust it.

fact: Camphor is distilled from the wood of Cinnamomum camphora; it is a topical analgesic and moth repellent, but swallowed camphor causes seizures, especially in children.
caution: Keep mothballs and camphor ointment away from children's mouths.
maomao_note: Rub it on and the ache fades. Swallow it and you fade. The skin is the correct door.

fact: Pufferfish liver and ovaries hold tetrodotoxin, which blocks voltage-gated sodium channels; there is no antidote, and in Japan only licensed cooks may prepare fugu.
caution: Tingling lips are the first sign; paralysis follows while the mind stays clear.
maomao_note: The one food that pays the cook more than the fisherman. I would like to try the liver once. Luomen says no. Luomen is usually right.

fact: Antivenom has been made since the 1890s by immunising horses with small venom doses and purifying the antibodies, a method pioneered by Albert Calmette.
caution: Do not cut, suck or tourniquet a bite; keep the limb still and get antivenom.
maomao_note: The snake is not the medicine. The horse that survived the snake is the medicine. Nature is indirect.

fact: Ox bezoar is a gallstone from cattle, composed largely of bilirubin and bile acids; it is among the most expensive traditional drugs and the key ingredient of Angong Niuhuang Wan.
caution: Costly, frequently adulterated, and a prescription drug in traditional practice.
maomao_note: A stone a cow was unhappy to carry, sold for its weight in gold to people who are unhappy in other ways.

fact: Gelsemium elegans contains gelsemine and related alkaloids that cause respiratory depression; it is a notorious poison in Chinese history and folklore, where it is called 'heartbreak grass'.
caution: Confused with edible vines and honeysuckle; no household use.
maomao_note: Named for what it does to the intestines, not the heart. The poets were being polite.

fact: Bitter apricot kernels contain amygdalin, which releases hydrogen cyanide when digested; traditional medicine uses small processed doses for cough, and poisonings from eating kernels as a 'health food' are well documented.
caution: A handful of bitter kernels can poison an adult; sweet culinary kernels are a different cultivar.
maomao_note: Smells like marzipan. So does the last breath of someone who ate too many. Count them.

fact: Hyoscyamus niger contains hyoscyamine and scopolamine; its seeds were burned as a painkiller in medieval Europe and it recurs in accounts of 'witches' ointments'.
caution: Same tropane picture as datura: dry, hot, blind and raving.
maomao_note: Everything it does, datura does too. Collectors still want both. I am a collector.
